digest.top_line: Guix HDR custom surface molds: 5-yr actuarial LC 98% (99% primary, 87% recurrent) for facial BCC/SCC, N=136, the most mature of today's skin brachy series.
digest.tldr: All five studies cover HDR surface/mould brachy for skin cancer, mostly face and head and neck, with high LC across series: 92% at 1 yr (Gogineni), 84.9% at 2 yr (Casey), 98% at 5 yr (Guix). Follow-up is short outside Guix, and the ABS survey shows no consensus on margins, dose or dosimetric constraints.

sites.intro: Single-institution HDR surface/mould series plus an ABS practice survey; none has a randomised comparator vs surgery or EBRT.

studies.name: Fractionated HDR brachytherapy moulds for carcinoma of the pinna (Allan)
studies.tldr: 13 superficial pinna carcinomas, HDR mould 45 Gy/8 fx over 5 days: complete resolution in all, no recurrence or late toxicity at minimum 18 mo f/u.
details: 🔍 Single-institution series (Christie Hospital), 13 pts treated up to July 1996

details.text: 🔍 Histology
subdetails: BCC: 9 pts
SCC: 3 pts
Intraepidermal carcinoma: 1 pt

details: 🔍 Lesions confined to pinna skin; dermal ultrasound confirmed no cartilage invasion in all but one

details.text: 💊 RT technique: HDR microselectron, single stepping iridium source
subdetails: Single-plane moulds: 45 Gy surface dose in 8 fx over 5 days
Twice-daily on 3 middle days, minimum 6 h interfraction interval
Ultrasound-measured full tumour thickness placed inside the 80% isodose surface
Sandwich mould (full-thickness pinna, 10 mm plane separation): dose reduced to 42.5 Gy

details.text: 📐 Dose falls to 80% of surface at 1.5-3.5 mm depth depending on source height; gradient ~10% per mm

details: 📊 Acute reaction: moderate erythema confined to high-dose area, settled by 6-wk first follow-up
📊 Complete tumour resolution in all pts; no recurrences, no late complications at minimum 18 mo
⚠️ Highly selected small series; no comparator arm, no formal toxicity grading reported in source
⚠️ BED comparison vs other regimens via LQ model; Table 2 row association uncertain in source extraction
⚠️ Minimum 18 mo f/u is short for late cartilage necrosis and BCC recurrence

verdict.rationale: Single-institution series of 13 highly selected pts, no comparator, short minimum follow-up, ungraded toxicity. Technique description more than outcome evidence.
verdict.audience: Superficial BCC/SCC of the pinna, cartilage not invaded

studies.significance: The transferable parameter is ultrasound-guided depth prescription: tumour thickness measured to sub-mm (0.84 mm in one case) set the source-to-skin height (5 vs 10 mm) so the 80% isodose covered tumour while sparing cartilage. That steep ~10%/mm gradient is the argument for a mould over electrons when lesions are thinner than a 4 MeV beam's 12 mm 90% depth.
studies.monday_clinic: In a small superficial pinna BCC or SCC with cartilage intact on imaging, this supports a custom HDR surface mould as a cartilage-sparing RT option; it does not inform cartilage-invading or full-thickness disease, where the sandwich-mould experience is a single case.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-institution case series and technique report from the Christie Hospital, **13 pts** treated up to July 1996. Design not stated as prospective.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Superficial cancers of the pinna **not invading cartilage** (9 BCC, 3 SCC, 1 intraepidermal). Dermal ultrasound confirmed cartilage intact in all but one.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: HDR microselectron moulds, **45 Gy in 8 fx over 5 days** for single-plane moulds, prescribed so the full ultrasound-measured tumour depth sits within the **80% isodose**. One full-thickness case used a sandwich mould at **42.5 Gy**; tungsten shielding was added for source heights above 5 mm when needed.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **Complete tumour resolution in all pts**, no recurrences and **no late radiation complications** over a minimum 18 mo follow-up. Acute moderate erythema stayed confined to the high-dose area and settled by the 6-wk visit.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The authors position moulds against electrons (unsuitable for lesions thinner than the 12 mm 90% depth of 4 MeV, risking cartilage necrosis), 30 kVp X-rays (hard to make uniform on curved surfaces, bone photoelectric risk) and surgery (amputation or graft, admission). No comparative outcome data are presented.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents small superficial pinna carcinomas with cartilage intact, measurable by dermal ultrasound. Does not represent cartilage-invading or bulky full-thickness disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: No formal toxicity grading or cosmesis scale; cosmesis was described as excellent by the treating team. The higher late-tissue BED is justified by small volume rather than by measured late outcomes.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The contribution is a **depth-tailored prescription**: ultrasound thickness sets source height, and the steep surface gradient lets dose fall off before cartilage. Whether that holds for larger lesions or longer follow-up is not settled here.

studies.interpretation:
This is best read as a technique paper with a small outcome audit attached, not as efficacy evidence. Its durable idea is that the prescription depth for a superficial ear lesion should be measured rather than assumed. By putting transdermal ultrasound in front of mould design, the authors turn tumour thickness into the variable that sets source-to-skin height, and with it the depth of the 80% isodose. In the worked examples, a lesion penetrating 0.84 mm was treated at a 5 mm height, while a thicker BCC reaching the cartilage surface used 10 mm. The cartilage is either partly or wholly outside the high-dose volume, which is the whole point on a structure the authors describe as poorly tolerant of high dose.

The argument against the alternatives is physical rather than clinical. Electrons are set aside because a pinna lesion is often thinner than 3 mm and laterally as small as 10 mm, well inside the build-up and penumbra behaviour of a low-energy beam. Kilovoltage at 30 kVp has the right depth dose but, in the authors' account, is hard to deliver uniformly over a curved surface and carries a bone risk from photoelectric absorption. Surgery is criticised on cosmesis and the need for admission. None of these comparisons is tested; they are reasons to choose the technique, not evidence that it outperforms the others. A modern reader would add that orthovoltage, electronic brachytherapy and conformal external beam with bolus have all changed since this was written, so the competitive frame is dated.

The outcome claims deserve calibrated confidence. Thirteen pts, described by the authors as highly selected, with complete resolution, no recurrence and no late complications at a minimum 18 months, is consistent with what one expects from small superficial BCC treated with an adequate dose, and it does not discriminate this technique from others. BCC recurrence and cartilage necrosis are both late events, so the minimum follow-up is the binding limitation. Toxicity was not graded on a named scale and cosmesis was judged by the treating team.

The fractionation choice rests on an LQ-model BED comparison that, by the authors' own reasoning, accepts a higher late-tissue BED than conventional fractionated regimens on the grounds that the irradiated volume is tiny. That is a reasonable volume argument but it is the exact assumption that longer follow-up would test. The single sandwich-mould case, where full-thickness irradiation was unavoidable and dose was lowered to 42.5 Gy, is where that assumption is weakest and the data thinnest.

What the paper leaves a practising radiation oncologist with is a workflow: image the depth, choose the height, keep cartilage outside the 80% surface, and fractionate HDR over a few days. That workflow transfers. The efficacy and late-toxicity numbers do not carry enough weight to choose this over other well-established superficial techniques.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The transferable parameter is ultrasound-guided depth prescription: measured tumour thickness set source height (5 vs 10 mm) so the 80% isodose covered tumour and spared cartilage. The ~10%/mm surface gradient is the case for a mould over electrons on lesions thinner than 3 mm.

open_questions: Late cartilage toxicity beyond 18 months with higher late-tissue BED
Outcomes vs electronic brachytherapy or orthovoltage for pinna lesions
Safety of full-thickness sandwich moulds in larger series

studies.name: Skin surface brachytherapy practice patterns survey (Likhacheva)
studies.tldr: 16 ABS respondents: margins 3-15mm (median 5mm), doses 30 Gy/5fx to 64 Gy/32fx (EQD2 40-65 Gy), no consensus on dosimetric constraints.
details: 🔍 30-question electronic survey of ABS clinician members; 16 complete returns from ~400 invitations
🔍 Practices: private, hospital, academic; aggregate experience 8 to 1800 cases
📊 60% routinely estimate lesion depth by ultrasound before treatment
📊 Median max prescription depth 5 mm (range 1 to 8 mm)
📊 Margin on gross disease: range 3-15mm, median 5mm

details.text: 📊 CTV margin adjustment
subdetails: Wider margin by histology: 70% of respondents
Squamous histology cited by 41%
Diffuse/morpheaform/aggressive BCC cited by 18%
Recurrent disease cited by 6%
Adjusted by lesion size: 65%

details: 📊 Hypofractionation preferred; 30 Gy/5fx to 64 Gy/32fx across scenarios (EQD2 40 Gy-65 Gy)
📊 Pretibial skin: 10 respondents (63%) used 2-3 Gy/fx; daily hypofractionated schedules avoided
📊 Size cut point for gentler fractionation: median 3 cm, range 2-5 cm

details.text: 📐 Dosimetric parameters endorsed for plan evaluation

details: 📐 Max allowable skin dose 125-150% (median 135%) of Rx; CTV coverage 90-100% (median 95%)
⚠️ Eight respondents reported severe acute/late toxicity on lower extremity, especially pretibial skin
⚠️ Common exclusions: tumor depth >3 mm, perineural invasion, prior RT
⚠️ n=16 from ~400 invited; self-selected responders, no outcome data, safety claim rests on recall

verdict.rationale: Small self-selected survey (16 of ~400 invited) with no outcome measurement; the 'convenient and safe' conclusion is not testable from practice-pattern recall.
verdict.audience: BCC and cSCC treated with skin surface brachytherapy

studies.significance: The usable signal is the pretibial outlier: eight respondents recalled severe toxicity on lower-extremity skin, and 63% de-escalated to 2-3 Gy/fx there. Nose lesions tolerated large fractions with little hesitation, so site, not histology, is where fractionation practice converges. The 3-15mm margin spread shows there is no shared CTV standard to benchmark against.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pretibial BCC or cSCC considered for surface brachytherapy, this supports gentler fractionation as community practice; it does not inform schedule choice for facial lesions on outcome grounds.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **30-question electronic survey** of American Brachytherapy Society clinician members. **16 complete returns** from approximately 400 invitations; one incomplete survey excluded. Responses also analyzed separately for practitioners with **>100 career cases**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Respondents nearly all US-based, one from Spain, split across private, hospital and academic practice. Aggregate experience ranged **8 to 1800 cases**. Survey addressed skin surface brachytherapy for **cSCC and BCC**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Shielded applicators most common, custom molds for large or curved areas; catheters placed 5 to 10 mm from skin, never directly on it. **Hypofractionation preferred**, with clinical-scenario doses from **30 Gy/5fx to 64 Gy/32fx (EQD2 40 Gy-65 Gy)**. Fractions increased for larger targets, with a size cut point of **median 3 cm (range 2-5 cm)**.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Margin on gross disease **3-15mm, median 5mm**; 70% widened margins by histology and 65% by size. Max skin dose limit **125-150% (median 135%)**, CTV coverage **90-100% (median 95%)**. No difference between experienced and less experienced responders (p=0.1539).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Eight respondents described **severe acute and late toxicity on the lower extremity, especially pretibial skin**. Three referred pts with non-healing in-field ulcers for hyperbaric oxygen. For pretibial targets, **10 respondents (63%) used 2-3 Gy per fraction**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: No prospective comparison is offered; respondents suggested **NCCN low-risk vs high-risk BCC/SCC definitions** for margin decisions. The authors call for prospective trials and expert consensus guidelines to reduce practice variation.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents dose, margin and planning habits of a small group of ABS brachytherapists treating BCC and cSCC. Does not represent outcome or toxicity rates, which were not measured.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Toxicity reported as anecdote, without denominators or grading. Clinical scenarios did not specify histology, so BCC vs cSCC dose selection cannot be separated.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Practice converges on **hypofractionation and pretibial de-escalation** and diverges on margins and plan-evaluation metrics. Volumetric metrics (D2cc, D1cc, D0.1cc) were endorsed by no respondent, so a dosimetric constraint set remains undefined.

studies.interpretation:
This paper is a census of habits, not a test of them, and its value depends on reading it that way. Sixteen practitioners out of roughly 400 invited is a small, self-selected sample, and the people who answer a skin brachytherapy survey are plausibly those most invested in the technique. That bias runs in a predictable direction: toward enthusiasm about convenience and safety. The authors' conclusion that skin brachytherapy can be convenient and safe should therefore be held loosely, because nothing in the design measures safety. Toxicity entered the dataset as recalled cases, without a denominator, a grading scale, or follow-up time.

What the survey does establish, with reasonable confidence, is where practice converges and where it does not. Convergence sits on two points. Hypofractionation is the default, and pretibial skin is treated differently: 10 respondents used 2-3 Gy per fraction there, and eight separately recalled severe toxicity on the lower extremity. That pattern is consistent with what radiation oncologists already believe about poorly vascularized lower-leg skin, and it is the one finding a reader could carry into practice as a shared community norm rather than one institution's preference. The almost uniform comfort with large fractions on a small nasal lesion is the mirror image.

Divergence is larger and arguably more informative. Gross-disease margins span 3 to 15mm. Plan evaluation is inconsistent: max skin surface dose is the most endorsed parameter, but minimum CTV dose was used by only half, and no respondent used D2cc, D1cc or D0.1cc. Many applicator users calculate to a single depth and look at no dose distribution at all. That means the field has no common dosimetric language with which to report outcomes, which in turn makes pooling retrospective series across institutions difficult. The suggestion to borrow NCCN low-risk and high-risk definitions for margins is a pragmatic workaround, not a validated rule.

The experience-stratified analysis showing no difference between practitioners above and below 100 career cases (p=0.1539) is underpowered to detect anything, so it should not be read as reassurance that technique is learned quickly.

The decision this informs is narrow. For a radiation oncologist starting or auditing a skin brachytherapy program, it offers a reference range for margins, depth and fractionation, and a clear warning about pretibial targets. It does not tell anyone which schedule controls tumor better or produces better cosmesis, and it predates any prospective comparison against EBRT or electronic brachytherapy. For it to be wrong in its central claim of safety, the unreported denominators would only need to be modest.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Pretibial skin is where practice converges: 63% used 2-3 Gy/fx and eight respondents recalled severe lower-extremity toxicity. Margins (3-15mm) and plan-evaluation metrics vary widely, so there is no shared dosimetric standard to audit a skin brachytherapy program against.

open_questions: Which skin brachytherapy fractionation optimizes control and cosmesis?
Standard dosimetric constraints for surface applicators and molds
Safe dose per fraction for pretibial lesions

studies.name: CT-based flap brachytherapy for facial NMSC (Gogineni)
studies.tldr: 1-yr KM local control 92% after 40 Gy/8 fx twice-weekly HDR flap brachy for T1 facial BCC/SCC; 49/53 lesions good/excellent cosmesis.

details.text: 🔍 Retrospective review, 50 pts / 53 lesions, treated Jan 2007 to Dec 2018
🔍 T1 (AJCC 8th) BCC or SCC, biopsy-confirmed; all NCCN high-risk (area H, or area M ≥10 mm)

details: 🔍 Selected case-by-case by multidisciplinary dermatology clinic, mostly surgery intolerance or refusal

details.text: 🔍 Cohort
subdetails: Median age 80 (73-101)
Median size 18 mm, median thickness 5 mm
48 (91%) primary, 5 (9%) recurrent

details.text: 💊 Technique
subdetails: 40 Gy/8 fx twice weekly, BED 60 Gy (α/β 10), Ir-192 HDR
CTV = visible tumor + 5 mm; PTV = CTV, no added margin
Catheter flap: channels 5 mm from surface, 10 mm apart, fixed in thermoplastic mask
5 mm spacer intranasal, under eyelid, or gingivolabial sulcus
Median PTV 1.7 cc, D90 92%, V100 85%

details.text: 📊 1-yr KM LC 92%; 4 local recurrences (2 nasal SCC, 1 eyelid BCC, 1 lip BCC)
📊 Toxicity
subdetails: Acute G1 60%, G2 35%, G3 5%; all after the 5th fraction
All 8 eyelid/periorbital pts: G1 conjunctivitis, resolved with antibiotic/steroid drops
Chronic G1 10% at 6 mo; G1 4% and G2 4% at 12 mo
No chronic G≥3, no treatment-related hospitalization

details.text: ⚠️ Median f/u 15 mo (6-27), too short to read out late BCC recurrence or late toxicity

details: ⚠️ Toxicity is reported inconsistently: abstract calls the 5% acute events G2 (Results says G3); Discussion reports no chronic G≥2, though 4% had chronic G2

details.text: ⚠️ Toxicity percentages track the 53 lesions, but the text labels them as pts
🔗 Other HDR surface-mold series in the paper report LC 87-100%

details: 🔗 The one cited face-BCC RCT (surgery vs RT, mostly interstitial BT) showed 4-yr failure 7.5% vs 0.7% favoring surgery

verdict.rationale: Retrospective single-arm series, 53 lesions, 15-mo median f/u; no comparator vs Mohs or EBRT. Consistent with prior HDR mold series.
verdict.audience: T1 facial BCC/SCC, NCCN high-risk, surgery declined or not tolerated

studies.significance: The transferable detail is the planning: CT-simulated flap in a glued thermoplastic mask, CTV tumor + 5 mm with no PTV margin, and a 5 mm spacer intranasally or under the eyelid. That combination delivered median D90 92% on 1.7 cc targets over nose, eyelid and ear. All 4 recurrences were in area H, 2 of them nasal SCC.
studies.monday_clinic: In an elderly pt with T1 area-H BCC or SCC who declines or cannot tolerate Mohs, this supports twice-weekly HDR flap brachy as a short-course definitive option; it does not address pts fit for and accepting surgery, or lesions beyond T1.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective review** of 50 pts with 53 facial NMSC lesions treated Jan 2007 to Dec 2018. LC estimated by **Kaplan-Meier**, response by clinical exam. Median f/u **15 mo** (range 6-27).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Biopsy-confirmed BCC or SCC, **T1 (AJCC 8th)**, f/u ≥6 mo; all NCCN high-risk by location. Median age 80; **75% area H**, nose most common (32%). Selected mainly for **surgery intolerance or refusal**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **40 Gy/8 fx twice weekly** HDR (BED 60 Gy, α/β 10) via silicone catheter flap, CT-planned in BrachyVision. **CTV = tumor + 5 mm, PTV = CTV**; prescription to cover ≥95% PTV within Emami-derived BED constraints. Median D90 92%, V100 85%.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **1-yr LC 92%**; 4 local recurrences, all in area H (2 nasal SCC, 1 eyelid BCC, 1 lip BCC). **49 lesions (92%)** had good/excellent cosmesis with complete remission.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Acute G1 60%, G2 35%, G3 5%, all after fx 5. Every eyelid/periorbital pt had G1 conjunctivitis. At 12 mo, chronic G1 4% and G2 telangiectasia 4%; **no chronic G≥3**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: LC sits within the **87-100%** range of other HDR surface-mold series the authors cite. The one cited face-BCC randomized trial favored surgery (4-yr failure 7.5% vs 0.7%), though RT there was mostly interstitial BT.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents elderly pts with T1 high-risk facial BCC/SCC who are not surgical candidates or decline surgery. Does not represent surgery-eligible pts, deeply infiltrating tumors, or lesions beyond T1.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Grade assignments disagree across the abstract, results and discussion. Toxicity percentages use the **lesion denominator** while being labeled as pts. Depth was assessed **clinically by palpation**, which matters for a prescription fixed at 5 mm from the flap surface. BCC and SCC were dosed identically.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The data support flap HDR as a feasible definitive option where Mohs is declined, delivering **8 visits** with acceptable cosmesis. Two questions stay open: durability beyond 1-2 yr, and whether nasal SCC needs a different dose or margin.

studies.interpretation:
The question this series answers is narrow: can a CT-planned catheter flap deliver a homogeneous, conformal HDR dose over the most irregular surfaces of the face, in an elderly population that has declined or cannot tolerate surgery, without unacceptable toxicity? On that question the answer looks favorable. Three-quarters of lesions sat in area H, a third on the nose, and the plans still reached a median D90 of 92% on targets of around 1.7 cc. That technical point is the real contribution, because the stated weakness of electron or orthovoltage EBRT on the nose, eyelid and ear is dose inhomogeneity over curved, small fields, and surface molds can lose skin contact on those same contours. The flap, glued into a thermoplastic mask, plus a 5 mm spacer for nasal, eyelid and lip lesions, is a reproducible setup another department could copy.

The efficacy claim needs more caution. A 1-yr Kaplan-Meier LC of 92% fits the 87-100% range the authors cite from other HDR mold series, but those series are also retrospective, and agreement among uncontrolled cohorts is weak corroboration. The cited randomized comparison in facial BCC showed more failures with RT than surgery at 4 yr, 7.5% vs 0.7%. RT in that trial was mostly interstitial brachytherapy, so it does not test this technique directly, but it is the only randomized anchor, and it points against RT where surgery is an option. With a median of 15 mo and a maximum of 27 mo, this cohort cannot yet show the late BCC recurrences that drive differences at 4-5 yr.

The pattern of failure deserves attention. All four recurrences were in area H, and two were nasal SCC, in a cohort where SCC made up a third of lesions. The authors dosed BCC and SCC identically, following NCCN, ASTRO and ABS guidance that does not separate by histology. A small series cannot settle whether nasal SCC needs a wider margin or more dose, but this is the subgroup to watch in larger datasets. Depth was assessed by palpation, and the median thickness was 5 mm under a prescription that depends on depth, so underdosing at depth is a plausible mechanism for failure in thicker central-face SCC.

The reporting has internal inconsistencies that lower confidence in the toxicity figures. The abstract and results disagree on whether the 5% acute events were grade 2 or 3. The discussion claims no chronic grade ≥2 toxicity while the results report grade 2 telangiectasia in 4%. Percentages track lesions while the text calls them patients. None of this changes the overall impression that late toxicity was mild, but a reader should not quote these exact numbers as settled.

For practice, this supports twice-weekly flap HDR as a short-course definitive option for elderly patients with T1 high-risk facial NMSC who will not have Mohs. It does not support offering RT over surgery to a fit patient, and it leaves open durability beyond about two years and histology-specific dosing.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The transferable detail is the planning: CT-simulated flap in a glued thermoplastic mask, CTV tumor + 5 mm with no PTV margin, and a 5 mm spacer intranasally or under the eyelid. That combination delivered median D90 92% on 1.7 cc targets over nose, eyelid and ear. All 4 recurrences were in area H, 2 of them nasal SCC.

open_questions: Local control and late toxicity beyond 2 years of follow-up
HDR flap brachytherapy vs Mohs for area-H NMSC
Histology-specific dose or margin for nasal SCC

studies.name: HDR brachytherapy with custom surface molds for facial skin carcinomas (Guix)
studies.tldr: 5-yr actuarial LC 98% overall (99% primary, 87% recurrent) with HDR Ir-192 custom PMMA surface molds for facial BCC/SCC, N=136.

details.text: 📊 Local control by presentation

details: 🔍 Prospective single-institution series, 136 consecutive facial BCC/SCC, treated 1992-1997
🔍 Gross tumor left in place in most pts; margins positive in 128

details.text: 🔍 Dose: 6000-6500 cGy in 33-36 fx of 180 cGy, prescribed at 5 mm depth
🔍 Lesions ≥4 cm: boost 1800 cGy/10 fx after 3-wk rest, total 7500-8000 cGy
🔍 Ir-192 HDR via 117 custom PMMA molds and 19 Brock applicators

details: 📊 Mold dose at surface and 5 mm depth within 5% of prescription; TLD agreed within 5%

details.text: 📊 Cosmesis good/excellent in 98% at 6 mo; no severe late complications reported
🔗 vs Lovett EBRT series: superficial X-ray LC 95% (180/189), electrons 77% (44/57)

details: ⚠️ Min f/u 12 mo; only 32 primary and 29 recurrent pts at risk at 5 yr

details.text: ⚠️ Internal inconsistencies in the source
subdetails: Boost 1800 cGy in Methods vs 1500 cGy in Fig 5 legend
Recurrent-tumor LC 87% given at 5 yr in Results, at 4 yr in Discussion
Diameter reported as average 3.8 cm, ranging 3.8 to 8.0 cm

verdict.rationale: Single-arm institutional series with no comparator vs Mohs or EBRT; only 3 events, thin 5-yr risk set, cosmesis formally scored only to 12 mo.
verdict.audience: Facial BCC/SCC, primary or recurrent after surgery, node-negative, M0

studies.significance: What transfers is the physics: optimized dwell times on a face-conformal PMMA mold held surface and 5 mm dose within 5% of prescription on curved sites, with a lead insert to spare the eye. That favors mold HDR over electrons on nose, eyelid and ear. The protracted 180 cGy/fx schedule is the part that dates.
studies.monday_clinic: In a facial BCC or SCC on a curved site such as the nose or eyelid, already planned for definitive RT, this supports a custom-mold HDR surface technique for dose conformity; it does not address RT vs Mohs, and control was lower in tumors recurrent after surgery.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prospective single-institution series of **136 consecutive pts**, treated March 1992 to February 1997, followed to March 1998 with a **minimum follow-up of 12 mo**. LC estimated by Kaplan-Meier. Cosmesis and toxicity were scored on SOMA-LENT at end of treatment, 6 mo and 12 mo.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Pathologically confirmed **BCC (102) or SCC (34) of the face**. **73 primary, 63 recurrent after previous surgery.** Average age 67. Margins positive in 128. No nodal or distant disease at diagnosis.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: HDR Ir-192 via **117 custom PMMA molds** (3-7 parallel catheters, 5-10 mm apart, 5 mm bolus layer) or 19 Brock applicators. **6000-6500 cGy in 33-36 fx of 180 cGy at 5 mm depth.** Lesions ≥4 cm got an **1800 cGy/10 fx boost** after a 3-wk rest, to 7500-8000 cGy total.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: All pts had G1-2 erythema at completion. **Ulceration at 6 wk in 14 pts (10%)**, mostly in boosted ≥4 cm lesions, and all healed by month 4. **No severe late complications.** Unfavorable long-term cosmesis was limited to recurrent tumors >4 cm.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Primary-tumor LC of **99%** is comparable to the superficial X-ray arm of Lovett's EBRT series (**95%**) and above its electron result (**77%**). Daly's Ir-192 implants reached **96%** LC but with severe long-term effects in **18%**.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents node-negative facial BCC/SCC treated definitively with gross disease in place, including recurrences after surgery. Does not represent nodal or metastatic disease, non-facial sites, or hypofractionated HDR surface schedules.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The source contradicts itself in places: **boost 1800 vs 1500 cGy**, and recurrent-tumor LC is given at 5 yr in one place and 4 yr in another. Depth of invasion was not determined, and with **3 events** no risk-factor analysis was possible.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The authors credit the absence of severe late effects to **180 cGy/fx** vs Lovett's **300-400 cGy**, but technique and selection confound that comparison. The dosimetric case for molds on curved surfaces is stronger than the comparative LC claim.

studies.interpretation:
The number a radiation oncologist should weigh is 99% actuarial local control at 5 years in previously untreated facial BCC and SCC, alongside 87% in tumors that had already recurred after surgery, with 3 local failures across 136 pts. Set against the external-beam series the authors lean on, Lovett's, the primary-tumor result sits alongside that series' superficial X-ray control of 95% and well above its electron result of 77%. Daly's iridium implant series reached 96%. The honest read is that a surface mold delivered through an HDR afterloader matches the best orthovoltage control rather than beating it. With 3 events, the series cannot distinguish 95 from 99, and a reader should not treat the gap as real.

The population is a fairer test than many skin RT series, because gross tumor was left in place in nearly everyone and margins were positive in 128 pts. This is definitive treatment of macroscopic disease, not adjuvant cleanup. Against that, the follow-up is shallow. The minimum is 12 months, and by 5 years only 32 primary and 29 recurrent pts remained at risk, so the 5-year actuarial figures rest on a thin tail. The recurrences that did occur fell at 17 and 23 months, inside the observed window, but late skin effects such as fibrosis, atrophy and telangiectasia evolve over years, and formal SOMA-LENT scoring stopped at 12 months. The claim of no severe late toxicity is therefore a medium-term claim. The paper is also internally inconsistent: the boost is 1800 cGy in the methods and 1500 cGy in a figure legend, recurrent-tumor control is placed at 5 years in the results and 4 years in the discussion, and the lesion diameter range starts at its own mean. None of this overturns the result, but it argues for reading the specific numbers loosely.

The schedule is where transferability breaks. A course of 33-36 fractions at 180 cGy, extended to 7500-8000 cGy with a boost after a 3-week break for lesions of 4 cm or more, is long for an often elderly skin cancer population, and current HDR surface practice has moved toward hypofractionation. The authors attribute their lack of severe late effects to the low dose per fraction compared with Lovett's 300-400 cGy. That is biologically plausible, but technique, era and case mix are confounded with fraction size here, and the series cannot isolate it.

What does transfer is the physical argument. Optimized dwell weights on a mold cast from the pt's own face kept dose at the surface and at 5 mm depth within 5% of prescription across curved anatomy, with a sharp edge gradient, TLD verification within 5%, and an embedded lead sheet to spare the globe. Electron and orthovoltage beams struggle with the non-flat nose, eyelid and ear, which together with the cheek made up much of this cohort. The decision this paper informs is technique selection for a facial lesion already headed to RT, not whether to choose RT over Mohs, which it never tested. The case for molds would be wrong if a comparative series on curved sites showed electrons with bolus achieving equivalent uniformity and control. The lower control and worse cosmesis in large recurrent tumors are the clearest signal that early referral matters more than technique.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Mold HDR held surface and 5 mm dose within 5% of prescription on curved facial anatomy, with a lead insert for the eye, which favors it over electrons on nose, eyelid and ear. LC was 99% in primary tumors but 87% in recurrent ones. The 180 cGy/fx schedule is the part that does not transfer to current hypofractionated practice.

open_questions: Hypofractionated mold HDR vs conventional 180 cGy fractions for late cosmesis
Mold HDR brachytherapy vs Mohs surgery for facial BCC/SCC
Predictors of local failure in tumors recurrent after surgery

studies.significance: The coverage detail is the RT read: wired target with no PTV, prescribed at 0.5 cm, median V100 only 73.7%, and 2-yr LC 76.9% when V90 <95% vs 88.9% above (NS). Three of five recurrences were nasal BCC, so target-margin and coverage choices on the nose are the parameter to tighten.
studies.monday_clinic: In an elderly pt with a superficial head and neck BCC or SCC who is not a surgical candidate, this supports HDR surface mould as a low-toxicity option; it does not address lesions deeper than 5 mm or pts fit for Mohs.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective** single-institution review at BC Cancer, Jan 2010 to Dec 2017, **59 pts / 65 lesions**. Median follow-up 8 mo (range 4.1-11.9). Univariate log-rank analysis of LC by dose-volume and tumor factors.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: All skin tumors treated with Ir-192 HDR surface mould; **BCC 54%, SCC 31%**, plus melanoma, lentigo maligna, Merkel, cutaneous NHL and one post-resection keloid. Median age 82 (range 45-97), mostly head and neck sites; 7 lesions palliative intent.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: CT-planned individualized mould, catheters ~1 cm apart, **prescribed at 0.5 cm depth** with intent 90% dose covering the wired target; **no PTV expansion**. Most common **40 Gy/10 fx** (48.2%); range 15 Gy/3 to 60 Gy/30. Median surface dose 126.5%, V90 92.3%, V100 73.7%.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **2-yr LC 84.9%**, CR 96.8%, 2-yr PFS 71.5%, 2-yr OS 77.6%. Local recurrence in 5 pts. No dose-volume or histology factor reached statistical significance for LC.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No G3-5 acute or late toxicity.** Acute G2 dermatitis 32% and ulceration 8%; one late G2 necrosis (2%) at ~10 mo. Late G1 mostly hypopigmentation 15.4% and fibrosis 8%.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Source places this against Gauden et al. (36 Gy/12 fx, **LC 98%** at median f/u 7 mo), other brachy series at **83.3% to 100%**, EBRT LC 87-100% and Mohs 95-99%. GEC-ESTRO grades the technique B because the base is small and retrospective.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents elderly, often comorbid pts with superficial head and neck skin cancer treated where surgery is unsuitable. Does not represent lesions deeper than 5 mm, surgically fit pts, or long-term late toxicity and cosmesis.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Histologies with very different biology (keloid, lymphoma, melanoma, Merkel) and palliative lesions are pooled into one LC estimate. Toxicity was graded from records and photos; cosmesis not reported. Internal discrepancies in age, follow-up and sex counts.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: LC sits at the low end of the brachy literature, and the BCC subgroup (**70%**) underperformed SCC (**88.2%**), the reverse of usual expectation. With V100 73.7% and no PTV, under-coverage at the lateral or deep edge is a plausible contributor the series cannot resolve.

studies.interpretation:
The case for surface mould brachytherapy in skin cancer has always been an argument about selection rather than efficacy. Surgery, and Mohs in particular at 95-99% local control in the figures this paper cites, sets the bar; radiotherapy earns its place in pts whose age, comorbidity, or tumor location makes resection a poor trade. This series is squarely in that space: a median age of 82, a cohort in which 20 pts had died at analysis mostly of unrelated causes, and a stated rationale that the modality was chosen because these were elderly pts. Read that way, the headline that matters most is the toxicity profile. No grade 3 or higher event, acute or late, in a frail population is the result most likely to hold up, and it is the one most relevant to the decision a radiation oncologist actually faces with an 85-year-old and a nasal lesion.

The control figures deserve more caution. A 2-yr local control of 84.9% sits below Gauden et al.'s 98% and near the bottom of the 83.3% to 100% range the authors quote for other brachytherapy series. Two features of this dataset push in opposite directions. First, the 2-yr estimates are actuarial projections from a median follow-up of 8 mo, so the true 2-yr figure could be lower once late recurrences accrue, particularly for BCC, which tends to recur slowly. Second, the cohort pools palliative lesions, lymphoma, melanoma and Merkel cell carcinoma with the BCC and SCC that make up the clinical question, which should depress control relative to a clean NMSC series. The authors report no difference with palliative cases excluded, but the sample is too small for that reassurance to carry much weight.

The more instructive signal is in the dosimetry. The plan prescribed to 0.5 cm, used no PTV margin on a wired clinical target, and achieved a median V100 of 73.7%. Lesions with V90 below 95% had 2-yr LC of 76.9% against 88.9% above that threshold, and BCC fared worse than SCC (70% vs 88.2%), with three of the five recurrences being BCC of the nose. None of this reached statistical significance, and with five events it could not have. Still, the pattern is coherent: a technique whose dose falls off steeply with depth, applied without margin to a histology known for subclinical extension, on a curved nasal surface where mould fit is hardest. That is a hypothesis about target definition, not a verdict on the modality, and it lines up with the debate the authors cite between prescribing to the wired CTV and adding a margin for setup and misalignment.

What would make the reassuring reading wrong is longer follow-up. Late necrosis appeared at about 10 mo, already near the edge of the observation window, and cosmesis, the outcome that most often justifies choosing brachytherapy over surgery on the face, is not reported. A reader should take from this series that surface mould HDR is tolerable in very elderly pts and that coverage and margin on nasal BCC merit scrutiny, not that its control matches surgery or EBRT.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: With no PTV and median V100 73.7%, LC tracked coverage numerically (76.9% vs 88.9% by V90 95% cut, NS). Nasal BCC carried 3 of 5 recurrences, which argues for margin and coverage scrutiny there when choosing surface mould prescription depth and target definition.

open_questions: Does LC hold beyond 2 years with mature follow-up?
Does a PTV margin or V90 ≥95% improve LC for nasal BCC?
Cosmetic outcomes vs electrons or EBRT in elderly pts
